Check that every bracket, brace and parenthesis in a string is closed by its own kind, in order.

Adapted from Exercism's [problem specification](https://github.com/exercism/problem-specifications/tree/main/exercises/matching-brackets) (MIT). Listed under [Parsing & Validation](/examples/?subject=parsing-and-validation).

```nomi-run
// FILE: matching_brackets.nomi
/// Whether every bracket, brace and parenthesis in `text` is closed by its
/// own kind, in the right order. Other characters are ignored.
pub fn paired?(text: String) -> Bool {
    balanced?(String.to_codepoints(text), [])
}

/// `awaited` holds the closer each open bracket waits for, innermost first.
fn balanced?(rest: List<Codepoint>, awaited: List<Codepoint>) -> Bool {
    case #(rest, awaited) {
        #([], _) -> awaited == []
        #(['(', ..rest], _) -> balanced?(rest, [')', ..awaited])
        #(['[', ..rest], _) -> balanced?(rest, [']', ..awaited])
        #(['{', ..rest], _) -> balanced?(rest, ['}', ..awaited])
        #([cp, ..rest], [next, ..awaited]) when cp == next -> balanced?(rest, awaited)
        #([')' or ']' or '}', .._], _) -> False
        #([_, ..rest], _) -> balanced?(rest, awaited)
    }
}

// FILE: matching_brackets_test.nomi
import matching_brackets

test "checks bracket pairing" {
    cases = [
        #("paired square brackets", "[]", True),
        #("empty string", "", True),
        #("unpaired brackets", "[[", False),
        #("wrong ordered brackets", "}{", False),
        #("wrong closing bracket", "{]", False),
        #("paired with whitespace", "{ }", True),
        #("partially paired brackets", "{[])", False),
        #("simple nested brackets", "{[]}", True),
        #("several paired brackets", "{}[]", True),
        #("paired and nested brackets", "([{}({}[])])", True),
        #("unopened closing brackets", "{[)][]}", False),
        #("unpaired and nested brackets", "([{])", False),
        #("paired and wrong nested brackets", "[({]})", False),
        #("paired and wrong nested brackets but innermost are correct", "[({}])", False),
        #("paired and incomplete brackets", "{}[", False),
        #("too many closing brackets", "[]]", False),
        #("early unexpected brackets", ")()", False),
        #("early mismatched brackets", "{)()", False),
        #("math expression", "(((185 + 223.85) * 15) - 543)/2", True),
        #(
            "complex latex expression",
            "\\left(\\begin{array}{cc} \\frac{1}{3} & x\\\\ \\mathrm{e}^{x} &... x^2 \\end{array}\\right)",
            True,
        ),
    ]

    subtests cases, #(description, text, expected), description {
        assert matching_brackets.paired?(text) == expected
    }
}
```

## How it's written

- The string is scanned as `String.to_codepoints`, so each bracket is a codepoint literal in a pattern (style guide §19).
- The stack holds the closer each open bracket waits for, so a closing bracket only has to equal the stack's head.
- One `case` over the pair `#(rest, awaited)` with list patterns. A first version matched `rest` alone and nested a `case awaited` in the closer arm; `fmt` then broke every arm of the outer `case` onto two lines, which hid the shape, so the pair form replaced it.
- One `subtests` table for all 20 cases.
- A closer that does not match the stack's head ends the scan: `#([')' or ']' or '}', .._], _) -> False`, an `or` pattern nested in the list pattern. A closer that does match is any codepoint equal to the head, since only closers are pushed. Matching the closer by name there too (`[')' or ']' or '}' as closer, ..rest]`) made the arm too long for one line, and `fmt` then broke every arm onto two lines.
